Title: Enhancing human-machine interaction: a novel approach to emotion-controlled speech-to-animation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for emotion-controlled speech-to-animation, addressing the issue of emotional mismatches between speech and facial expressions in existing methods. Our approach synchronises emotional expression across audio and facial animations using State-of-the-Art (SOTA) pretrained models, eliminating the need for costly custom training while ensuring adaptability. A key contribution of our framework is the creation of a novel a Speech-to-Speech (S2S) pipeline for emotional control over generated speech. In addition, we introduce a novel evaluation metric, the Emotion Distribution Divergence (EDD), to assess our models ability to modify the emotions in the original videos. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in emotional expressiveness and realism over existing methods, establishing our approach as a major advancement in human-machine interaction, virtual assistants, and emotion-aware IoT applications.

Title: Sign Language to Spoken Language Translation: Models and Techniques
Abstract: For deaf and hard-of-hearing populations, sign language is a crucial means of communication, but a significant gap exists for those without proficiency in it. Automatic sign language to spoken language translation systems provide promising solutions that enable real-time interpretation in readable form and foster inclusivity. This paper summarizes recent developments and approaches in sign-to-speech generation. Input representations such as transfer learning, glove-based, and vision-based techniques are examined, along with widely used machine learning architectures like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Preprocessing challenges, dataset requirements, and essential post-processing techniques, including error correction and language modeling, are also discussed to improve accuracy. To bridge the communication gap in diverse contexts, the paper highlights applications of this technology in daily life and proposes future directions for developing scalable and accessible sign language translation systems adaptable to different languages and dialects.

Abstract: This paper presents a novel AI-powered Smart Navigation System designed to enhance the mobility and independence of visually impaired individuals. Traditional navigation aids such as guide dogs, white canes, and GPS systems provide limited situational awareness and lack real-time environmental feedback crucial for safe navigation. Our system integrates advanced computer vision technology using the YOLOv8 model to enable real-time detection of obstacles, such as pedestrians and vehicles, while offering additional functionalities like traffic light recognition and weather alerts. Speech-to-speech communication transforms visual data into auditory cues, empowering users with immediate and actionable information. Field tests demonstrate that the system significantly improves navigation safety and user confidence, offering a transformative solution in assistive technology. This research highlights the potential of artificial intelligence to revolutionize support for the visually impaired, providing a comprehensive platform for safe and informed navigation in dynamic environments.

This platform is capable to handle more than 50 languages online as well as offline mode when downloaded with the supported language packs. This puts a strong emphasis on user data privacy. Instead of switching between different applications, this system allows uniquely a smooth conversation to a natural flow of response in one second. The testing shows that the system achieves a strong accuracy of translation with having BLEU score of more than 40 and user satisfaction levels exceeding 90%. This paper outlines the system design and its flutter-based user interface which is helpful in hybrid cloud edge architecture for discussion in social benefit and potential for scaling the speech translation technique.

Title: EmojiVoice: Towards long-term controllable expressivity in robot speech
Abstract: Humans vary their expressivity when speaking for extended periods to maintain engagement with their listener. Although social robots tend to be deployed with "expressive" joyful voices, they lack this long-term variation found in human speech. Foundation model text-to-speech systems are beginning to mimic the expressivity in human speech, but they are difficult to deploy offline on robots. We present EmojiVoice, a free, customizable text-to-speech (TTS) toolkit that allows social roboticists to build temporally variable, expressive speech on social robots. We introduce emoji-prompting to allow fine-grained control of expressivity on a phase level and use the lightweight Matcha-TTS backbone to generate speech in real-time. We explore three case studies: (1) a scripted conversation with a robot assistant, (2) a storytelling robot, and (3) an autonomous speech-to-speech interactive agent. We found that using varied emoji prompting improved the perception and expressivity of speech over a long period in a storytelling task, but expressive voice was not preferred in the assistant use case.

Title: UTRo-NAST: Non-Autoregressive Speech Translation via Understanding, Translation, and Reordering
Abstract: Non-autoregressive speech translation (NAR-ST) has attracted increasing attention due to its ability to deliver competitive translation quality with faster inference speed. However, further improving the performance of NAR-ST models remains a challenging and important research direction. To this end, we propose UTRo-NAST, a novel NAR-ST framework that decomposes speech translation into three consecutive subtasks: source speech understanding, word-level translation, and target-side word reordering. The model first encodes the source speech into high-level acoustic representations, which are then translated into a sequence of target words. Finally, the sequence is reordered to match the syntactic and grammatical structure of the target language. By modularizing the speech translation pipeline, UTRo-NAST enhances model interpretability, robustness, and overall performance. Experiments on the MuST-C benchmark across eight language pairs show that UTRo-NAST consistently outperforms existing NAR-ST models and achieves translation quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines, while maintaining faster decoding speed. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed framework for practical speech translation.

Title: Adversarial Speech-Text Pre-Training for Speech Translation
Abstract: Large-scale pre-training has been shown to benefit speech translation tasks. However, existing multimodal pre-training efforts rely on parallel corpora for semantic alignment, potentially limiting performance to the scale of available data and causing data imbalance. Hence, we propose an adversarial speech-text pre-training (AST) scheme for speech translation. This scheme aligns the feature distributions of speech and text modalities instead of enforcing semantic alignment based on parallel corpora. Specifically, we introduced a dual-stream mechanism that bridges speech and text modalities through speech, text, and shared encoders. In addition, we designed an adversarial bridging method that focuses on the differences in feature distributions between speech and text. Leveraging a discriminator and hidden state-level swapping strategy emphasizes semantic information in speech representations, while avoiding the limitations imposed by the scale of parallel corpora. We applied AST to both end-to-end speech translation and large model architectures. Experimental results on the IWSLT test sets demonstrate that AST improved the performance of speech translation models and is compatible with large language models.

Title: SPlice: Automated Testing for Speech Translation via Syntactic Analysis
Abstract: With the advancement of Deep Learning, the performance of speech translation systems has made remarkable progress. However, similar to traditional software, speech translation systems can still suffer from software defects that can lead to incorrect translations with potentially serious consequences. These systems are also vulnerable to real-world environmental interference, making their behavior unpredictable. The black-box nature of deep neural networks renders traditional testing methods ineffective, while the lack of diverse test cases and the challenge of constructing test oracles further hinder the implementation of their testing. To address this, we introduce syntactic structure invariance, a linguistically inspired concept that captures the structural containment between a pair of derivationally related sentences and their corresponding translations. Based on this concept, we propose a novel speech translation testing method, SPlice. SPlice simulates environmental disturbances on a seed speech, disassembles it into a template and speech blocks, and then generates multiple derivational speech pairs by inserting the blocks back into the template. SPlice detects translation errors by checking whether the syntactic structure invariance relation is violated in the translation results corresponding to the speech pairs. To validate SPlice, we experiment with three industrial speech translation systems: Google Translate, Youdao Translator, and Iflytek Translator. With 600 speeches crawled from the BBC as seed tests, SPlice detects 1,640, 1,101, and 1,305 translation errors with around 90.7% precision. The experimental results show that SPlice can effectively detect errors in the speech translation results with high precision, providing valuable information for developers to improve system performance.

Title: Semi-Supervised Knowledge Distillation Framework towards Lightweight Large Language Model for Spoken Language Translation
Abstract: Even though large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across various natural language processing tasks, their application in speech-related tasks has largely remained underexplored. This work addresses this gap by incorporating acoustic features into an LLM which can be fine-tuned for downstream direct speech-to-text translation and automatic speech recognition tasks. To address the computational demands associated with fine-tuning LLMs, a novel self and semi-supervised knowledge distillation technique is proposed to implement a lightweight LLM having 50% lesser parameters. Validated on the MuST-C and Librispeech datasets, this technique achieves over 92% of the performance of the larger LLM, demonstrating both robust performance and computational efficiency.

Title: A Domain-Specific Multilingual Speech Translation Corpus via Simultaneous Interpretation
Abstract: This paper presents a novel multilingual speech translation corpus for complex, domain-specific content in Korean, English, Spanish, and Japanese. The corpus contains 4,000 hours of parallel speech, including 1,000 hours of Korean audio with simultaneous sight interpretations in the other three languages by 294 professionals (242 interpreters and 52 Korean voice actors). It also includes transcriptions, translations, and annotations for all languages. The Dewey Decimal Classification was adapted to balance knowledge representation, and speech tasks were conducted in a controlled studio environment to ensure data consistency. Translation, transcription, and annotation workflows were managed through a custom-built platform. The corpus captures nuanced contexts, cultural sensitivities, and domain-specific terminology, addressing linguistic challenges like structural differences between SOV (Korean, Japanese) and SVO languages (English, Spanish). Preliminary evaluations indicate its potential to enhance end-to-end speech translation models, support cross-lingual transfer learning, and tackle real-time translation issues.

Title: Voice-guided Orchestrated Intelligence for Clinical Evaluation (VOICE): A Voice AI Agent System for Prehospital Stroke Assessment
Abstract: We developed a voice-driven artificial intelligence (AI) system that guides anyone—from paramedics to family members—through expert-level stroke evaluations using natural conversation, while also enabling smartphone video capture of key examination components for documentation and potential expert review. This addresses a critical gap in emergency care: current stroke recognition by first responders is inconsistent and often inaccurate, with sensitivity for stroke detection as low as 58%, causing life-threatening delays in treatment. Three non-medical volunteers used our AI system to assess ten simulated stroke patients, including cases with likely large vessel occlusion (LVO) strokes and stroke-like conditions, while we measured diagnostic accuracy, completion times, user confidence, and expert physician review of the AI-generated reports. The AI system correctly identified 84% of individual stroke signs and detected 75% of likely LVOs, completing evaluations in just over 6 minutes. Users reported high confidence (median 4.5/5) and ease of use (mean 4.67/5). The system successfully identified 86% of actual strokes but also incorrectly flagged 2 of 3 non-stroke cases as strokes. When an expert physician reviewed the AI reports with videos, they identified the correct diagnosis in 100% of cases, but felt confident enough to make preliminary treatment decisions in only 40% of cases due to observed AI errors including incorrect scoring and false information. While the current system’s limitations necessitate human oversight, ongoing rapid advancements in speech-to-speech AI models suggest that future versions are poised to enable highly accurate assessments. Achieving human-level voice interaction could transform emergency medical care, putting expert-informed assessment capabilities in everyone’s hands.

Title: Enhancing Accessibility Through Machine Learning-Based Sign Language to Speech Translation
Abstract: For people with speech and hearing impairments, sign language is an essential communication tool; however, there are frequently obstacles when engaging with non-sign language speakers. In order to improve accessibility and inclusivity, this work suggests a real-time framework for speech translation and Indian Sign Language recognition. The Random Forest algorithm is used by the system to classify gestures based on finger spelling, utilizing machine learning techniques. Cameras record hand gestures, which are then preprocessed using techniques like hand segmentation and background filtering. To create efficient training and testing datasets, discriminative features, such as hand orientation and position, are taken out of these. After the classifier predicts the gesture class, a text-to-speech module converts the gesture class into verbal output. The system facilitates smooth communication between sign language users and non-users by combining gesture recognition and speech synthesis. For real-time sign language-to-speech translation, the suggested method shows promise as a reliable, effective, and scalable solution that will greatly advance the creation of intelligent assistive technologies.

Title: Multimodal AI for Seamless Communication: Integrating Computer Vision and Speech Translation with LLMs
Abstract: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI) dramatically enhances linguistically and visually AI-aided communication. This study proposes a new framework integrating computer vision, speech translation and large language models (LLMs) for context-sensitive and real-time communication. The proposed system employs computer vision for scene comprehension and text capturing, speech translation for real-time multilingual conversation, and LLMs for comprehension and response generation. Combining these technologies enhances interaction between machines and humans, provides assistive technology solutions for people with disabilities and aids communication in different languages in various settings. In this work, the framework utilises a multi-stream fusion strategy to enable coherent and pertinent responses to be generated during information processing across various modalities. A system benchmark evaluation confirmed the system's effectiveness in speech-to-text, image-to-text and multilingual voice recognition tasks instead of classical single-modality methods. Benchmark results show a BLEU score of 41.24, outperforming mBART and the Transformer baseline, while remaining competitive with M2M-100. The results emphasise the role of multimodal AI in overcoming communication barriers and their drastic use in educational purposes, as well as in healthcare, customer relations, and international settings and collaborations.

Title: Spatial Speech Translation: Translating Across Space With Binaural Hearables
Abstract: Imagine being in a crowded space where people speak a different language and having hearables that transform the auditory space into your native language, while preserving the spatial cues for all speakers. We introduce spatial speech translation, a novel concept for hearables that translate speakers in the wearer’s environment, while maintaining the direction and unique voice characteristics of each speaker in the binaural output. To achieve this, we tackle several technical challenges spanning blind source separation, localization, real-time expressive translation, and binaural rendering to preserve the speaker directions in the translated audio, while achieving real-time inference on the Apple M2 silicon. Our proof-of-concept evaluation with a prototype binaural headset shows that, unlike existing models, which fail in the presence of interference, we achieve a BLEU score of upto 22.01 when translating between languages, despite strong interference from other speakers in the environment. User studies further confirm the system’s effectiveness in spatially rendering the translated speech in previously unseen real-world reverberant environments. Taking a step back, this work marks the first step towards integrating spatial perception into speech translation.

Title: NEXUS-O: An Omni-Perceptive and -Interactive Model for Language, Audio, and Vision
Abstract: Human beings perceive the real world through a spectrum of sensory modalities, encompassing auditory, visual, and linguistic faculties. This work proposes an industry-level omni-modal large language model (LLM) pipeline that integrates auditory, visual, and linguistic modalities to overcome challenges such as limited tri-modal datasets, high computational costs, and complex feature alignments. Our pipeline consists of three main components: First, a modular, end-to-end framework enabling flexible configuration of various encoder-LLM-decoder architectures. Second, a lightweight training strategy that pre-trains audio-language alignment on the state-of-the-art vision-language model Qwen2.5-VL, thus avoiding the costly pre-training of vision-specific modalities. Third, an audio synthesis pipeline that generates high-quality audio-text data from diverse real-world scenarios, supporting applications such as Automatic Speech Recognition and Speech-to-Speech chat. Title: i-LAVA: Insights on Low Latency Voice-2-Voice Architecture for Agents
Abstract: We experiment with a low-latency, end-to-end voice-to-voice communication model to optimize it for real-time conversational applications. By analyzing components essential to voice to voice (V-2-V) system viz. automatic speech recognition (ASR), text-to-speech (TTS), and dialog management, our work analyzes how to reduce processing time while maintaining highquality interactions to identify the levers for optimizing V-2-V system. Our work identifies that TTS component which generates life-like voice, full of emotions including natural pauses and exclamations has highest impact on Real time factor (RTF). The experimented V-2-V architecture utilizes CSM1b has the capability to understand tone as well as context of conversation by ingesting both audio and text of prior exchanges to generate contextually accurate speech. We explored optimization of Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) iterations by the TTS decoder which come at a cost of decrease in the quality of voice generated. Our experimental evaluations also demonstrate that for V-2-V implementations based on CSM most important optimizations can be brought by reducing the number of RVQ Iterations along with the codebooks used in Mimi.

Title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting for Speech Translation
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable advancements in language understanding and generation. Building on the success of text-based LLMs, recent research has adapted these models to use speech embeddings for prompting, resulting in Speech-LLM models that exhibit strong performance in automatic speech recognition (ASR) and automatic speech translation (AST). In this work, we propose a novel approach to leverage ASR transcripts as prompts for AST in a Speech-LLM built on an encoder-decoder text LLM. The Speech-LLM model consists of a speech encoder and an encoder-decoder structure Megatron-T5. By first decoding speech to generate ASR transcripts and subsequently using these transcripts along with encoded speech for prompting, we guide the speech translation in a two-step process like chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is used for the T5 LLM for model adaptation and shows superior performance to full model fine-tuning. Experimental results show that the proposed CoT prompting significantly improves AST performance, achieving an average increase of 2.4 BLEU points across 6 En→X or X→En AST tasks compared to speech prompting alone. Additionally, compared to a related CoT prediction method that predicts a concatenated sequence of ASR and AST transcripts, our method performs better by an average of 2 BLEU points.

Title: Bridging Disfluent to Fluent in Speech Translation: Effective Tagging and Fine-Tuning Strategies
Abstract: Speech translation (ST) converts speech into text or speech in the target language. A major challenge in ST is handling spontaneous speech, which often includes disfluencies such as fillers and hesitations. Fluent translations enhance readability, clarity, and usability, making disfluent-to-fluent (D2F) ST highly desirable. Generally, fine-tuning with parallel data in ST is effective, but for D2F ST, limited training data constrains performance. To mitigate the data scarcity issue in D2F ST, we explore training strategies for a disfluency-aware ST model, utilizing augmented data with disfluency tagging and multi-stage fine-tuning. Our experiments show that leveraging disfluency tagging and multi-stage fine-tuning significantly improves performance while reducing disfluencies in translation.

Title: Granite-speech: open-source speech-aware LLMs with strong English ASR capabilities
Abstract: Granite-speech LLMs are compact and efficient speech language models specifically designed for English ASR1 and automatic speech translation (AST). The models were trained by modality aligning granite-3.3-instruct to speech on publicly available open-source corpora. Title: Fine-Tuning SeamlessM4T Moroccan Darija to Classical Arabic Speech Translation
Abstract: This study investigates the fine-tuning of SeamlessM4T, a multilingual speech-to-text translation model, to enhance its performance in translating Moroccan Arabic (Darija) speech into Classical Arabic text. Due to Darija’s linguistic complexity, which includes borrowed vocabulary and phonetic variability, conventional speech recognition and translation systems struggle to achieve high accuracy. By fine-tuning SeamlessM4T on the Darija-C corpus, this work aims to optimize the model’s ability to handle dialectal speech. The evaluation, based on BLEU scores, demonstrates a significant improvement in translation accuracy after fine-tuning. The results highlight the potential of SeamlessM4T for low-resource dialect translation while also identifying challenges related to phonetic variations and domain adaptation. This research contributes to advancing speech translation for underrepresented Arabic dialects and provides insights into optimizing neural architectures for dialectal speech processing.

Title: VaaniVerse: Low-Latency Speech Translation Using Universal Earphones
Abstract: In multilingual societies like India, language barriers are a major obstacle to effective communication. Due to their reliance on internet connectivity, high cost, poor performance in noisy environments and high latency, existing solutions frequently fail. This paper introduces VaaniVerse, a real-time, multilingual speech translation system with low latency that can be operated with smartphones and standard earphones. The system also integrates an efficient pipeline for speech-to-text (STT), text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis noise cancellation and context-free translation. VaaniVerse provides accurate and adaptable translations between Hindi, English and Kannada even in noisy environment using lightweight edge AI models like Whisper, Coqui TTS and IndicTrans2. Given that the architecture is optimized for offline use, accessibility and affordability are ensured. The system also futher incorporates several GUI-based novelties that enhances usability and distinguishes it from existing translation applications.

Title: A Modular-based Strategy for Mitigating Gradient Conflicts in Simultaneous Speech Translation
Abstract: Simultaneous Speech Translation (SimulST) involves generating target language text while continuously processing streaming speech input, presenting significant real-time challenges. Multi-task learning is often employed to enhance SimulST performance but introduces optimization conflicts between primary and auxiliary tasks, potentially compromising overall efficiency. The existing model-level conflict resolution methods are not well-suited for this task which exacerbates inefficiencies and leads to high GPU memory consumption. To address these challenges, we propose a Modular Gradient Conflict Mitigation (MGCM) strategy that detects conflicts at a finer-grained modular level and resolves them utilizing gradient projection. Experimental results demonstrate that MGCM significantly improves SimulST performance, particularly under medium and high latency conditions, achieving a 0.68 BLEU score gain in offline tasks. Additionally, MGCM reduces GPU memory consumption by over 95% compared to other conflict mitigation methods, establishing it as a robust solution for SimulST tasks.

Title: Indian Sign Language Recogniser with Text and Speech Translation
Abstract: Sign Language is important to bridge the gap between communication for the deaf and hard-of-hearing community. Here, we work with ISL in the context of the Indian deaf community. However, one of the major challenges here lies in making the interaction of ISL users with non-sign language users smooth. The system introduces a strong vision-based Indian Sign Language Recogniser with real-time text and speech translation for better communication and inclusiveness. It is made up of a system that uses deep learning models constructed on a TensorFlow backend, which classifies static ISL gestures captured through real-time video streams. OpenCV is utilized for hand detection and feature extraction to allow for accurate and efficient hand gesture recognition. The system translates recognised gestures into their corresponding textual representations and into audible speech, allowing the user for thorough comprehension by non-ISL users. It offers a user-friendly interface, including functionality such as activation of recognition, textual display, and speech synthesis.

Title: Zero-resource Speech Translation and Recognition with LLMs
Abstract: Despite recent advancements in speech processing, zero-resource speech translation (ST) and automatic speech recognition (ASR) remain challenging problems. In this work, we propose to leverage a multilingual Large Language Model (LLM) to perform ST and ASR in languages for which the model has never seen paired audio-text data. We achieve this by using a pre-trained multilingual speech encoder, a multilingual LLM, and a lightweight adaptation module that maps the audio representations to the token embedding space of the LLM. We perform several experiments both in ST and ASR to understand how to best train the model and what data has the most impact on performance in previously unseen languages. In ST, our best model is capable to achieve BLEU scores over 23 in CoVoST2 for two previously unseen languages, while in ASR, we achieve WERs of up to 28.2%. We finally show that the performance of our system is bounded by the ability of the LLM to output text in the desired language.

Title: Lost in Translation, Found in Context: Sign Language Translation with Contextual Cues
Abstract: Our objective is to translate continuous sign language into spoken language text. Inspired by the way human interpreters rely on context for accurate translation, we incorporate additional contextual cues together with the signing video, into a new translation framework. Specifically, besides visual sign recognition features that encode the input video, we integrate complementary textual information from (i) captions describing the background show, (ii) translation of previous sentences, as well as (iii) pseudo-glosses transcribing the signing. These are automatically extracted and inputted along with the visual features to a pre-trained large language model (LLM), which we fine-tune to generate spoken language translations in text form. Through extensive ablation studies, we show the positive contribution of each input cue to the translation performance. We train and evaluate our approach on BOBSL – the largest British Sign Language dataset currently available. We show that our contextual approach significantly enhances the quality of the translations compared to previously reported results on BOBSL, and also to state-of-the-art methods that we implement as baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate the generality of our approach by applying it also to How2Sign, an American Sign Language dataset, and achieve competitive results.

Title: FPCRL: Feature Projection and Contrastive Representation Learning for End-to-End Speech Translation
Abstract: Speech-to-text translation is a cross-modal and multilingual translation task. To alleviate the modality gap and data scarcity of this task, recent research has primarily focused on aligning speech and text representations to unify cross-modal features and incorporating external knowledge via multi-task learning. Although significant progress has been achieved, there remains potential for improvement, particularly in enhancing translation performance by purifying speech representations to extract more content-relevant information. In this paper, we propose a framework based on feature projection and contrastive representation learning for speech translation, FPCRL, which is adaptable to various training settings. FPCRL introduces additional full-content and irrelevant-content encoders, which separately extract full and irrelevant information from speech. Through a feature projection module, irrelevant components are removed from the full content representations, yielding purified speech representations. Furthermore, the extracted contentirrelevant information is utilized to guide the training of the irrelevant-content encoder via contrastive representation learning. Experiments on the MuST-C En-De, CoVoST-2 De-En, and CoVoST-2 Fr-En benchmarks demonstrate that FPCRL achieves significant improvements across all datasets.1

Title: Voice Craft: A Voice to Voice Conversion Framework
Abstract: Voice conversion technology has made great leaps with the incorporation of machine learning, which allows for effortless conversion of speech without losing the speaker's distinctive features. With the use of deep learning, it is now feasible to change the tone, style, and speech habits of a target speaker while retaining the linguistic content of a source speaker. VoiceCraft presents a novel voice-to-voice conversion strategy that leverages advanced neural architectures to deliver high-fidelity speech transformation. In contrast to conventional statistical approaches, which tend to falter when preserving naturalness, this system uses convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for feature extraction, transformers for phoneme mapping, and generative adversarial networks (GANs) for natural voice synthesis. The system starts with the extraction of fundamental voice features from both the source and target speakers. A pretrained speaker embedding model like Wav2Vec or ECAPA-TDNN captures distinctive vocal features, so the output voice is a true representation of the target speaker's tone and style. A phoneme alignment module then creates accurate mappings between the source and target voices, maintaining clarity and consistency in the translated speech. Deep neural networks also fine-tune speech features, such as prosody, pitch, and intonation, to produce a natural and expressive output. To make the overall speech sound more quality, a neural vocoder such as WaveNet or HiFi-GAN synthesizes high-resolution waveforms, so the voice produced sounds natural and smooth. The broad variety of applications, such as speech synthesis, voice dubbing, assistive communication devices, and AI-powered virtual assistants. By providing individualized and adaptive voice conversion, the system adds value to user experiences in entertainment, accessibility, and interactive AI systems. Future development will be directed towards real-time processing, cross-lingual voice conversion, and enhanced robustness in variable acoustic environments. Increasing the dataset and using self-supervised learning methods can further increase adaptability, with the result being more accurate and efficient voice conversion across languages and dialects.

Title: Optimizing Speech Multi-View Feature Fusion through Conditional Computation
Abstract: Recent advancements have highlighted the efficacy of self-supervised learning (SSL) features in various speech-related tasks, providing lightweight and versatile multi-view speech representations. However, our study reveals that while SSL features expedite model convergence, they conflict with traditional spectral features like FBanks in terms of update directions. In response, we propose a novel generalized feature fusion framework grounded in conditional computation, featuring a gradient-sensitive gating network and a multi-stage dropout strategy. This framework mitigates feature conflicts and bolsters model robustness to multi-view input features. By integrating SSL and spectral features, our approach accelerates convergence and maintains performance on par with spectral models across multiple speech translation tasks on the MUSTC dataset.

Abstract: With the rapid development of multilingual speech translation technology, cross-linguistic communication has gradually become an important demand in the era of globalization, especially for the translation of minority languages, where technological breakthroughs are particularly crucial [4]. Title: Speak Sign: ISL to Multilingual Speech Using Deep Learning Framework
Abstract: This research proposes a Hybrid Bi-LSTM with Attention Mechanism for Speak Sign: ISL to Multilingual Speech, leveraging a deep learning framework. Previous approaches for gesture recognition and sign-to-text translation, including CNN, GRU, LSTM, GRU-LSTM, LSTM-GRU, BiLSTM, and Bi-LSTM with Attention, primarily relied on static features or linear sequential models, which are limited in capturing complex spatiotemporal dependencies. To overcome these limitations, the proposed model integrates a Bi-LSTM with an attention mechanism to capture bidirectional temporal trends and emphasize key frames through attention weighting. This combination enhances sequential recognition of ISL gestures and improves sentence formulation. Experimental results on a personalized ISL dataset show that the proposed system outperforms GRU by 0.5 %, LSTM by 0.4 %, GRU-LSTM by 0.4 %, LSTM-GRU by $\sim 0.3 \%$, and Bi-LSTM by $\sim 0.3 \%$ in Accuracy, Precision, and Recall, demonstrating improved robustness and generalization for real-time ISL-to-speech translation.

Title: Enhancing Web Accessibility for Mathematics Through Semantic Enrichment of MathML
Abstract: Mathematical expressions pose significant challenges to web accessibility, particularly for individuals relying on assistive technologies (AT). While MathML (Mathematical Markup Language) has long been a standard for representing mathematics on the web, its adoption remains limited due to inconsistent browser support. In this paper, A novel approach is introduced to enhance MathML accessibility by semantically enriching Presentation of MathML using heuristics. This enrichment generates a semantic tree embedded within the MathML structure, enabling more accurate aural rendering and improved interaction with assistive devices. The complexities of text-to-speech translation for mathematics are explored, addressing the unique challenges of rendering symbols, punctuation, and complex layouts. The proposed method ensures that all elements of the mathematical expression are preserved for both visual and aural representation, offering a more inclusive experience. Additionally, the integration of this semantic enhancement with tools like MathJax is discussed, providing a robust solution for delivering accessible mathematics content across browsers.

Title: GestureSpeak: A Real-Time Sign to Speech Translation
Abstract: Speech disorders can significantly hinder verbal communication, making sign language an essential tool for individuals to convey information. While most studies have concentrated on American Sign Language (ASL) for motion and gesture recognition, there is a noticeable lack of focus on Indian Sign Language (ISL), which includes dialects such as English, Marathi and Hindi. This paper emphasizes the importance of developing an effective system for recognizing and converting ISL gestures into text, with a specific focus on addressing the challenges posed by complex hand movements and finger configurations. By utilizing the latest progress in computer vision and deep learning, we introduce a live recognition system that not only translates ISL gestures into text but also detects related emotional contexts. This system improves accessibility and inclusivity for sign language users, especially those with hearing impairments, by eliminating the need for a human translator. Our method provides a scalable solution to overcome communication barriers and promote enhanced social inclusion for the deaf community.

Title: IndicST: Indian Multilingual Translation Corpus For Evaluating Speech Large Language Models
Abstract: The integration of speech modalities into large language models, known as Speech LLMs, is a promising area of research for applications like automatic speech recognition (ASR) and automatic speech translation (AST). While several datasets exist for ASR, there is a critical gap for AST tasks in Indian languages. To fill this gap, we introduce IndicST, a new dataset tailored for training and evaluating Speech LLMs for AST tasks (including ASR and TTS), featuring meticulously curated, automatically and manually verified synthetic data. The dataset offers 10.8k hrs of training data and 1.13k hrs of evaluation data. Additionally, we present a scalable data collection methodology that allows easy development for other speech tasks. Our analysis examines the performance of various Speech LLMs on ASR and AST tasks, accompanied by insightful findings. We also explore the performance of these models across different prompts, highlighting the significant potential of our research in enhancing ASR and AST capabilities for Indian languages.

Title: Real Time Dynamic Sign Language Recognition System with LLM-Based Sentence Formation
Abstract: The need for a dynamic sign language recognition with speech translation has been addressed by the proposed work which presents efficiency and low-latency in American Sign Language (ASL) recognition. The method proposed in the work has leveraged the use of MediaPipe to expand a 1,680dimensional feature vector, including 18 novel spatial distances representing various gestures with capturing the difference in them. The usage of custom self-made dataset consisting of 2,400 video like image frame sequence (120 sequences × 20 ASL words × 30 frames) has been utilized. The Additive Temporal Attention Mechanism has been implemented in Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1D CNN) focusing on gesture-defining frames out of which the accuracy of 96.7% with inference latency under 500ms is achieved. The integration of on-premise Large Language Model (LLM) does the conversion into fluent grammatically correct sentence from the recognized keywords/signs by the system which are the speech-synthesized resulting into a complete end-to-end communication pipeline.

Title: Signify: Real-Time Two-Way Indian Sign Language Translation App
Abstract: The Signify system addresses the communication gap between the deaf, hard-of-hearing, and hearing populations in India by enabling real-time, bidirectional translation between Indian Sign Language (ISL) and spoken/text language. Designed for India’s 6.9 million deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals, the mobile application recognizes ISL gestures through the smartphone camera and translates them into text and synthesized speech, while also converting speech or text into animated ISL gestures. The core gesture-recognition model is a Random Forest ensemble, selected for its balance of accuracy and efficiency on mobile hardware. In preliminary evaluations, the system achieved robust classification accuracy, approaching the performance of recent CNN-based ISL solutions (~91%), while maintaining low computational overhead. Key features include multilingual support, 3D avatar-based sign rendering, and user-personalized gesture libraries. The main contributions of this work are: (i) a unified architecture for speech-to-sign and sign-to-speech translation, (ii) an intuitive and lightweight mobile interface, and (iii) a scalable, community-driven dataset expansion framework. Signify demonstrates the potential of practical, accessible, and inclusive ISL communication tools for everyday use.

Title: Research on Unified Speech Generation Method Based on Prompt Learning
Abstract: In recent years, Prompt Learning has demonstrated significant effectiveness in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Its core idea is to guide pre-trained large models to complete specific downstream tasks by designing appropriate prompts. This paradigm is increasingly being adopted in the speech processing domain, particularly in speech generation tasks. This paper systematically explores the practical value and inherent challenges of applying Prompt Learning to speech generation tasks, emphasizing its crucial role in improving the quality of speech generation and enhancing task adaptability. Based on an analysis of the characteristics and requirements of speech generation tasks, we propose a Prompt-based speech generation framework that effectively integrates both textual and speech information, enabling a unified approach to multiple speech generation tasks. The results demonstrate that Prompt Learning methods offer significant advantages in tasks such as speech translation and speech restoration, improving not only the naturalness and accuracy of generated speech but also the system’s flexibility and controllability. Furthermore, this paper discusses the challenges currently faced by the technology and provides an outlook on future research directions, offering valuable theoretical insights for the further development of speech generation technology.

Title: A Multi-Task Learning and Multi-Head Attention Based Sentiment Analysis Model for Interactive Edutainment Devices
Abstract: Multicultural and history education is key to fostering empathy, inclusiveness, and global understanding in young students. It enriches ideas, drives economic growth, and preserves cultural heritage. To promote global cultural education, we propose a solution using big data and smart technology through crane machines equipped with dolls dressed in traditional costumes. These dolls are interactive, collecting text and speech data from users. By using sentiment analysis, we can better understand the emotional and interactive needs of users. We introduce a text sentiment analysis model based on multi-head attention and multi-scale CNN. The data undergoes preprocessing, and BERT generates word vectors. BILSTM and multi-attention mechanisms capture contextual dependencies, while multi-scale CNNs extract local text features to detect sentiment polarity. These features are fused to create a new feature vector for prediction. Additionally, we propose an end-to-end speech sentiment analysis model (EML) based on multi-task learning. Speech is processed through the Wav2Vec2.0 pre-training model to obtain temporal feature representations. In training, the model simultaneously performs speech translation and sentiment classification. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of this approach.

Title: Bridging Speech and Text Foundation Models with ReShape Attention
Abstract: This paper investigates cascade approaches bridging speech and text foundation models (FMs) for speech translation (ST). We address the limitations of cascade systems which suffer from the propagation of speech recognition errors and the lack of access to acoustic information. We propose a ReShape Attention (RSA) that bridges speech embeddings of Whisper, a speech FM, to LLaMA2, a text FM. Speech and text embeddings have temporal and dimensional gaps, which make merging them challenging. RSA reshapes the speech and text embeddings into a sequence of subvectors sharing the same feature dimension. RSA performs cross-attention in the LLaMA2 layers between these two sequences, which allows combining the two embeddings. The RSA allows text FM to directly access speech FM embeddings and optimize the entire ST system for input speech. RSA improves 8.5% relative BLEU score compared to the baseline ST system, which cascades Whisper and LLaMA2. Moreover, our analyses show that the proposed method could even improve performance with ground-truth transcriptions, which suggests that our bridging approach is not limited to mitigating the effect of recognition errors but can also exploit the benefit of acoustic information.

Title: Research on Speech Alignment Algorithms for Big Data-Driven Online Translation Platforms
Abstract: With the acceleration of globalization, real-time speech translation has become a core requirement for cross-language interaction. As a key module, speech alignment's accuracy directly impacts system performance. To address the limitations of existing methods in noisy environments, low-resource languages, and real-time performance, this paper proposes a speech alignment algorithm that integrates multi-scale feature extraction with a dynamic attention mechanism (MSAM-BDA). This algorithm captures different time-frequency features through multi-resolution convolution, combines dynamic attention with adaptive feature weighting, and employs a cross-lingual transfer loss to improve adaptability to low-resource languages. Experimental validation on a 1000-hour multilingual corpus (MSPC) demonstrates that the MSAM-BDA achieves an alignment error rate (AER) of 3.21 %, a 5.31 percentage point reduction compared to DTW and a 0.94 percentage point reduction compared to BiLSTM. The algorithm also achieves a processing speed of 3420 frames per second, with a 30-second speech latency of only 118ms, meeting real-time requirements. Even under extreme noise (SNR = -5dB), the AER remains at 5.40%, with a noise attenuation rate of 68.5%, significantly outperforming competing algorithms. This algorithm provides an efficient and robust speech alignment solution for online translation systems.

Title: Classification VS Few-Shot-Learning Model for Translating Sign to Speech
Abstract: This research explores the application of computer vision and deep learning techniques to recognize American Sign Language (ASL) gestures and translate them into spoken language. Communication is fundamental to human interaction, and for individuals who are deaf or hard-of-hearing, sign languages like ASL are their primary mode of communication. However, a substantial communication barrier often exists between ASL users and the general hearing population, potentially leading to social exclusion and limited access to various opportunities. Recent advancements in computer vision, machine learning, and deep learning offer promising avenues to bridge this gap through the development of automated sign language recognition and speech translation systems. This study specifically addresses the challenges of data scarcity and the need for adaptable recognition systems in ASL. The proposed system utilizes a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for gesture classification, integrated with OpenCV for real-time hand detection, and an ASL recognition system that employs prototypical networks for few-shot learning. This comprehensive approach aims to facilitate communication for the deaf and hard-of-hearing community. Furthermore, the integration of Text-to-Speech (TTS) technology enables seamless conversion of recognized signs into spoken language. Experimental results demonstrate high recognition, accuracy and real-time performance, contributing significantly to the development of effective assistive communication devices.

Title: SSL400 - A Comprehensive Word Level Dataset for Sinhala Sign Language Recognition
Abstract: In the context of increasing digital accessibility and the need for inclusive communication technologies, the demand for automated sign language recognition has grown significantly. However, Sinhala Sign Language (SSL), used by the Sri Lankan deaf community, remains underexplored due to the lack of labelled datasets and the challenges of developing recognition models for low-resource languages. This study addresses this gap by introducing an SSL dataset, specifically curated to support real-time recognition of 384 commonly used words in daily and work-related contexts. The methodology for dataset creation involved expert consultations, a structured data collection process, and multi-step labelling. These steps ensured the accurate labeling of video data, which can be used for machine learning tasks like gesture recognition, sentence formation, and speech translation. The proposed dataset lays the foundation for SSL recognition models that are fast, lightweight, and optimized for low-resource environments. Additionally, we explore the performance of initial recognition models using this dataset, demonstrating its applicability in real-world scenarios. The dataset and research outcomes provide valuable resources for the development of inclusive AI-driven communication tools for the Sinhala-speaking deaf community. This contribution addresses the pressing need for better technological support for underrepresented languages in the field of sign language recognition and processing.

Title: Deploying a Residual Recurrent Neural Network for Robust Face Recognition and Emotion Detection with Multimodal Feature Fusion
Abstract: The recognition of facial emotions plays a crucial role in future multi-cultural visual communication systems, facilitating emotion translation across different cultures, similar to the way speech translation operates. If computers can recognize and respond to human non-verbal signals, such as emotions, the interactions between people and machines will feel more natural and seamless. Developing a robust facial descriptor that provides greater distinction for face recognition and enhanced detail for emotion analysis presents a significant challenge. While various methods are utilized to identify human emotions based on facial expressions or speech there has little research focused on integrating these modalities along with others to enhance the accuracy and reliability of emotion recognition systems. In this research, a multimodal face recognition and emotion analysis framework is proposed with the help of advanced deep learning techniques. This model processes diverse multimodal inputs, including face images, speech signals, and Electroencephalography (EEG) signals to effectively recognize emotions. All these inputs are gathered from standard sites before the implementation process. Initially, from the gathered face images, textual features are retrieved and denoted as feature set 1. The speech signals are processed to extract Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) and denoted as feature set 2. EEG signals are analyzed to extract wave features to form feature set 3. These extracted features from the three modalities are fused and fed into the proposed Residual Recurrent Neural Network (Res-RNN) for identifying various emotional states by recognizing the faces. Comprehensive evaluations are conducted to demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed model.

Title: The influence of reverberation, equalization and compression methods on speaker recognition
Abstract: The subject of the study is to analyze the impact of reverberation, compression and equalization methods on the accuracy of speaker speech detection. In recent years, the significance of audio preprocessing has grown considerably due to its crucial role in tasks such as data compression, filtering, and noise reduction. With the increasing demand for audio information classification, evaluating and comparing different preprocessing techniques has become essential to assess the accuracy and efficiency of the resulting solutions. This study focuses on examining how various audio preprocessing methods affect the accuracy of speaker speech detection, which is critical for subsequent neural network training. Particular emphasis is placed on methods of transforming audio signals into features, specifically using low-frequency cepstral coefficients. To achieve this objective, the study involved analyzing signal-to-feature transformation techniques and mathematical models used for audio sequence analysis based on the extracted features. A generalized real-time speaker speech translation model was developed, and an experiment was designed according to the selected audio preprocessing stages. The experiment was simulated by training and testing a convolutional neural network. The following methods were used: mel-frequency cepstral analysis, spectral analysis, mathematical methods of artificial intelligence. The following results have been obtained: depending on the chosen methods of pre-processing voice information and different ways of converting the signal into features, 86% accuracy of speaker’s language detection was achieved. The practical value of this work lies in expanding the range of audio files that can be used for training neural networks, as well as enabling translation of the resulting text into a selected language, including constructed or artificial languages. This study explored how different audio preprocessing techniques influence the accuracy of detecting a speaker’s speech, which is vital for subsequent neural network training involving various signal-to-feature transformation methods. The findings indicate that, in cases where audio recordings contain echoes, applying equalization can help reduce the echo effect.

Title: Real-Time Multilingual Communication System Using CNNs for Bidirectional Sign and Speech Translation
Abstract: A person who is proficient in Indian Sign Language cannot currently converse with someone who is proficient in sign languages from other countries. Additionally, there isn't an interface that translates between Indian Sign Language and other regional languages in India. The World Federation of the Deaf estimates that there are as many as seventy million people in the world using sign languages. It is the only way that the deaf people can express their feelings and emotions. Availing this language for the hearing and speech impaired is indeed of great significance to those who are learning as it shows the intent behind the expression and gives guidance on the person’s signing right away. The proposed solution aims to develop an interface that would close the communication gap that exists within the sign language community. Their ability and self-assurance in communicating with others through sign language can be enhanced by this. The system combines numerous machine learning models operating in the background with multiple translations, sign-to-sign, speech-to-sign, and sign-to-speech. These are employed to distinguish and identify the signs and convert them into the necessary spoken or sign language. These models are combined with a website that runs well to carry out the necessary translations. The system processes additional translation fast and effectively after receiving real-time video input. The goal of this research is to create a useful tool for converting between sign languages. Additionally, we may convert a specified sign language into a text or speech. translated from ASL to ISL with an 82% accuracy rate on average. To identify the indicators, our system receives video data in real-time. With our technology, a dumb or deaf person can converse with a blind person. Since our technology recognizes signs in real time, it may also be utilized by someone who wishes to learn sign language.
